title: Carlsen Wins Blitz Tiebreaker On Day 1 Of Total Chess Pilot
summary:
GM Magnus Carlsen is off to a promising start in the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 after winning the Blitz Tiebreaker with 7/9. GM Maxime Vachier-Lagrave finished second (6.5 points) and GM Levon Aronian third (6 points). The tournament started with a nine-round Swiss to have tiebreaks in place before the next nine days of competition.

Day two, which features rounds one and two of the Group Stage, is on Wednesday, November 11, starting at 9 a.m. ET / 15:00 CET / 7:30p.m. IST.

Blitz Tiebreaker Final Standings

(See full standings)

The Total Chess World Championship is the modern attempt to marry three time controls with one consolidated title: the FIDE World Combined Champion. While chess has separate classical, rapid, and blitz world champions, until now we have not crowned one player who can prove their versatility in all three formats. The 17th World Champion Ding Liren said that it is a "brand-new competition similar to the triathlon in athletics."

This iteration is a test run, but in 2027 FIDE will crown its first champion. The tour, which starts in March 2027, is expected to be an annual series; each year, four tournaments will funnel four qualified players to the Grand Final. Each leg will feature 24 players, just like the Pilot we are covering here. Experienced chess fans will recognize aspects of the Champions Chess Tour, Grand Chess Tour, and Freestyle Chess Grand Slam Tour in the description.

Let's break down the (rather complicated) format of the tournament piece by piece. Or, if you'd rather just skip to the day's action, you can navigate to the second bullet point right away and reference the format section later.

Total Chess Format Explained

Blitz Tiebreaks: Carlsen Is Back

Total Chess Format Explained

Blitz Tiebreaks

Each leg begins with Blitz Tiebreaks, which is what we cover on day one here. On the one hand, this stage won't decide too much, but on the other, it could have a veritable impact in what comes next. The rankings in the Blitz Tiebreaker, which is a nine-round Swiss tournament with all 24 players at a 3+2 time control, are used as the tiebreaker in the Group Stage. That is, if players finish with the same number of points in the next stage, how they did in the Blitz tournament matters. (It also has an effect on the Knockout Stage, but we explain that lower down.)

Group Stage

The groups were drawn at the opening ceremony, which took place just before the Blitz tournament. The 24 players were divided into four groups of six players each. Drawing of lots determined the placements, and the top four rated players by standard rating were intentionally placed into different groups.

Image: Courtesy of Total Chess.

The Group Stage is a double round-robin. Everybody plays two games a day against each player, and the Group Stage lasts five days. Everybody plays 10 games at this stage, and the time control is the new 45+30 "fast classic." One more thing: the scoring system is skewed to reward wins over draws, so a win is worth three points, a draw one point, and a loss zero.

Knockout Stage

After the Group Stage, all the players are ranked 1-6 based on how they did. The winners of each group advance to Knockout Bracket 1, second place to Knockout Bracket 2, and so on. Semifinal pairings in each Knockout Bracket are determined by their pre-tournament blitz rank among those four and paired 1–4 and 2–3.

It gets a little complicated, so bear with me here. Each match (Final, Semifinal, 3rd Place) takes two days and features all three time controls. They play four blitz games, two rapid games, and one fast classic game. A win in blitz is 1 point (0.5 for a draw), a win in rapid is 4 (2 for a draw), and a win in fast classic is 8 (4 for a draw).

The players switch colors on day two and do it all again, but here's the unusual part: the match score resets. The player who won on day one is the "day winner," but the margin by which they won isn't relevant for the second day. Let's say Player A wins day one, Player B wins day two; the players have an even score even if Player A won by a greater margin. That player does get to pick their color in the armageddon game (10 minutes for Black, seven for White, with a one-second increment starting on move 41).

Each Knockout Bracket is single-elimination and has a Final and Semifinals. The players who lose the Semifinals will still play in a match for third place. The winner of Knockout 1 is understood to win the event, and they earn the maximum number of points, 30. The Knockout 2 winner earns 20, the Knockout 3 winner earns 16, and so on.

Table: Courtesy of Total Chess.

The Grand Final

After four legs, we will then have four players who advance to the Grand Final based on the points they earned in the four legs. On that alone, this system sounds a lot like the Grand Chess Tour. Rather than dive into the format of that now, we can just say that the sole winner of that event is the FIDE World Combined Champion. Note that the rules may change based on learnings in the 2026 pilot tournament.

Blitz Tiebreaks: Carlsen Is Back

Twenty-four players participate in the 2026 pilot for the FIDE Total Chess World Championship. They represent the world's elite and qualified through several pathways set by FIDE and Norway Chess.

World number-one Carlsen, who chose not to defend his world championship title in 2023, is the star player in the field. His interest in classical chess has declined, but the faster time controls in this world championship are certainly more appealing for him.

Carlsen and Vachier-Lagrave were the two players to highlight on day one of the event. The blitz tournament serves as a low-stakes warm-up but may also have an effect later. A look at the standings gives us some idea of who's in good form, but there are nine more days. So the blitz tournament is anything but conclusive.

Read on, but you may also want to check out world number-two GM Hikaru Nakamura's video recap of the day.

Carlsen picked up wins against GMs Jan-Krzysztof Duda, Richard Rapport, Arjun Erigaisi, Anish Giri, and Haik Martirosyan (in that order), made four draws (GM Hans Niemann was one of those), and lost zero games. It's not to say that he wasn't in trouble; but, evidently, he slipped out of every bad position he got.

Carlsen told TV 2, "Whenever I could play on instinct, it was pretty good. Whenever I couldn’t play on instinct, it was pretty bad... “Sometimes you can get by on a bit of ‘hustle’ and momentum, and that’s what I did today.”

Carlsen won round one against Duda. Photo: Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

The story of round two could have been about Rapport, who defeated GM Fabiano Caruana in round one and outplayed Carlsen from the black side of a King's Indian Defense in round two. But in the time scramble, the Norwegian turned the position around and won.

After a draw with Vachier-Lagrave, Carlsen beat Arjun in round four. There, he showcased cold-blooded calculation to judge that 28...Rh6??, which threatens the pawn on h2, is what the late GM Daniel Naroditsky liked to call a "paper tiger." The threat had no real teeth, and Carlsen grabbed the free knight.

In the last round, a draw would have been good enough to share first with Vachier-Lagrave, but Carlsen managed to convert the pawn-up endgame (which, objectively, could be held). 43...Nd4? allowed Carlsen to show off the king's capacity to attack, at least when the coast is clear.

Carlsen was glad to win, but he didn't think it will make a difference in the long term. He said, "It’s extremely unlikely that anyone will finish tied when there are three points for a win. It doesn’t make much difference to the tournament, but it’s still nice to win.”

Vachier-Lagrave was Carlsen's closest competitor, several times being tied in the lead and once taking sole lead. That came after GM Vladislav Artemiev hung his rook in round five in an otherwise equal endgame, while Carlsen made a draw with GM Ian Nepomniachtchi.

Vachier-Lagrave scored wins against GMs Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, Vincent Keymer, Nepomniachtchi, Artemiev, and in round eight, Alireza Firouzja. He made three draws and lost one game against Arjun.

The battle of French numbers one and two. Photo: Photo: Michal Walusza/Total Chess.

Our Game of the Day is MVL's tactical brawl with Nepomniachtchi in round four, where he played the black pieces in a Rossolimo Sicilian. Black launched a decisive attack with a temporary knight sacrifice, and his powerful bishops raked across the board. GM Rafael Leitao goes over the full game below.

We are now set for the Group Stage, and we know who has the best tiebreaks. On Wednesday, we will see rounds one and two played with the fast classic time control, 45+30.

How to watch?

You can review the event on the Chess24 Twitch or YouTube pages. You can find the games on our dedicated events page. There was no stream for day one, but we will embed the stream here starting on day two.

The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot 2026 takes place on November 10-21 at the Anantara New York Palace Hotel in Budapest, Hungary. The event is a trial run for the official event in 2027, which will crown the first FIDE World Combined Champion. The event consists of a round-robin group stage and a knockout combining blitz, rapid, and fast classical time controls. The time control is 3+2 for blitz, 15+10 for rapid, 45+30 for fast classical, and 10 minutes (White) vs. 7 minutes (Black) with a one-second increment starting on move 41 in armageddon.

title: AAce_Cracker Stages Comeback In 2nd Gambit Cup
summary:
AAce_Cracker, a veteran who has played nearly 60,000 hands of poker on Gambit.com (where he was named Player of the Month in August and September), won the second special edition of the Gambit Cup, held on November 9. He outlasted a field of 1,359 players.

The winner beat satviksharma7777 in the heads-up final. Satviksharma7777 had dominated the final table until AAce_Cracker’s two pair turned the tables. Earlier, mehedi_AA had been eliminated in third place. The tournament, which was free to enter and offered no cash prizes, began at 12 p.m. ET / 6 p.m. CET / 10:30 p.m. IST and lasted just over two hours.

Top Finishers

WFM Alexandra Botez returned as live commentator, this time alongside professional player Landon Tice, who has won more than $4 million in live tournaments. In the first edition, two months ago, Botez was joined on the livestream by IM Danny Rensch, who played the part of the fans and asked technical questions about the game, which Botez answered effectively. The Gambit.com poker community has grown, and so has its knowledge. Even Elo ratings are starting to carry weight, and Tice’s explanations rose to the occasion.

The American player put the participants’ decisions into context, decisions that were especially complex in a turbo tournament that, despite the massive turnout, was decided in just over two hours.

Poker Tips

Tice kept giving the fans advice. He recommended that they be very patient, offered tips on bet sizing and defending the blinds, and urged them to be aggressive and not play scared. A very common mistake, as both he and Botez noted, is “limping”: entering the pot before the flop by simply calling the big blind instead of raising. Still, poker is a game of adapting to circumstances. “One lesson I learned early on is that sometimes you can win more by playing defensively,” said Tice, “by just calling against small bets.”

In chess, players can’t see the evaluation bar or the engine’s analysis, as viewers can. In poker, the players are far more in the dark than the viewers watching the broadcast, since they don’t even know their opponents’ hands. Botez was surprised every time a player folded the best hand. “It’s very common,” Tice explained. “It depends on who makes the first aggressive move and how the action unfolds. That’s why it’s important to know your opponents.” And that is why it is not unusual to see big bets made with the worst hand win the pot.

Of course, chance has its quirks. This hand between ugly_and_i_know… and MrChuckmate was full of twists. The former, holding K♥K♣, flopped a set of kings, an extremely strong hand. Then, on the turn, MrChuckmate (T♣J♣) completed a miraculous straight with the Q♦. But the river reversed the outcome again, giving Ugly a full house that proved truly ugly for his opponent.

A funny hand. The three of a kind was beaten by the straight, which in turn lost to the final full house.

Shortly afterward, MrChuckmate was rewarded for his battle against the kings when he cracked Samdekok's K♣K♦ with his Q♥J♦, hitting a straight on the turn. At that point, just over 30 players remained, and most of them had very few big blinds left, so their room to maneuver was very limited.

The broadcast was right to show so many of MrChuckmate’s hands. He escaped elimination when just 12 players remained, as his A♠Q♥ split the pot against fouchew5574’s A♣K♥. In the end, he went out in fifth place, which is nothing to complain about.

One of the most exciting hands of the day came soon after, with MrChuckmate out of the action for once. NameT4k3n was dealt A♠A♣ and went all-in, and was called by fouchew5574 with T♦T♠ and ArchieLootera with A♥J♥. On the flop (2♥5♥T♥), fouchew5574 hit a set and Archie picked up a heart flush draw. A lucky 2♠ on the river gave fouchew5574 a full house, though he was eliminated shortly afterward, in eighth place.

These were the five players who made it to the final table.

Five players reached the final table, all of them short-stacked. Even so, satviksharma7777 went on a run that seemed to be heading toward victory, rebuilding his stack to more than 40 big blinds. The turning point came in the heads-up final, when AAce_Cracker, holding 6♣2♠, flopped two pair that held up all the way to the river. Satviksharma7777, with top pair, could not bring himself to fold, and the momentum swung completely. He never recovered. A few hands later, AAce_Cracker took the title.

Alexandra Botez was surprised when she saw the winner’s stats. AAce_Cracker has a rating of 2165, has played more than 58,000 hands, and has taken 39 lessons. There is no doubt that he takes learning poker very seriously.

How to watch?

You can watch the day's broadcast on Chess.com's YouTube or Twitch channels.

The broadcast was hosted by WFM Alexandra Botez and poker player Landon Tice.

The Gambit Cup is a daily poker tournament hosted on Gambit.com, Chess.com's educational, gambling-free poker website. On August 31, IM Danny Rensch and WFM Alexandra Botez hosted a special edition of the event, which is free to enter. Members compete for the coveted Queen Gambit crown—a unique flair that goes on the winner's profile picture for the day. Finishing at the top also nets players tournament points to help them climb the Player of the Month leaderboard for bragging rights.

title: Movahed Stays Strong Ahead of Speed Chess Championship
summary:
Titled Tuesday (TT) on November 10 came down to tiebreaks between GMs Denis Lazavik and Sina Movahed, two players who also figure to feature prominently in the upcoming Speed Chess Championship (SCC), and it was ultimately Movahed who grabbed first place. The win was his fourth in Titled Tuesday this year, joining GM Jan-Krzysztof Duda at the top of the year's TT wins list.

While the SCC field is already decided, Titled Tuesday continues to contribute to the 2026-27 CCT Standings and 2027 Esports World Cup qualification. Movahed is now in second place behind GM Hikaru Nakamura, with Lazavik in third.

Broadcast

Recap

Movahed was one of 16 players to start on 4/4, but Lazavik had already made two draws and was only on 3/4. While it didn't stop him from tying for first, the slightly slower start may have cost him the tiebreaks.

In the fifth round, Movahed lost to GM Christopher Yoo, but a seventh-round draw was the only other blemish on Movahed's record. It was actually another Iranian player, GM Amin Tabatabaei, who became the biggest threat to this week's $6,000 perfect score bounty. He reached 7/7 with impressive wins like his fifth-round victory over GM Karthikeyan Murali, where he gained a solid edge via tactical means on moves 18-21 and converted without issue.

Two rounds after that, Tabatabaei defeated GM Alexey Sarana in round seven. Despite falling behind on the clock early, he made up that time deficit and more, and then won with better endgame play. But that would be the end of his lead, which a third under-30 Iranian star, GM Parham Maghsoodloo, claimed next. Their eighth-round game turned on moves 33-37 before ending on move 40.

Maghsoodloo's next win was even more impressive, taking the black pieces and outplaying Nakamura in an endgame while retaining a clock advantage throughout. By now, only GM Sam Sevian was within half a point, and Maghsoodloo next got White in their matchup.

And here the tide would turn once again. Sevian played slowly but solidly, and, like the tortoise against the hare, his steady approach paid off with a victory.

Sevian now led outright, and was a victory in the last round away from winning the tournament, with White against Lazavik. On the next board, Maghsoodloo tried to recover with Black against countryman Movahed. One of these four players was going to win the tournament.

Sevian almost immediately misstepped, however, with 12.Nf5, following a GM Ben Finegold rule and looking strong, but failing to 12...Qa5. Meanwhile, Movahed was taking a small edge over Maghsoodloo, then a big one once Maghsoodloo self-forked with 18...Nf5 and 19...Rf8. Suddenly, however, Sevian was surviving, but the pressure was still on after Movahed sealed the deal in his game:

Lazavik soon recouped his earlier gains, and the game came down to a time scramble, but Lazavik converted cleanly.

Even if his win delivered first place to Movahed, Lazavik's second place was a strong finish. Sevian's nine points stayed good enough for sixth place and a handful of CCT points. GMs Dmitry Andreikin, Sarana, and Jeffery Xiong finished in the three spots ahead of him, with Nakamura and GM Alexander Grischuk also scoring nine points to take seventh and eighth. Maghsoodloo and GM Dmitrij Kollars also picked up a CCT point to wrap up the top 10. WIM Margarita Potapova won the women's prize.

title: Abdusattorov, Sindarov Top Tata Steel Chess 2027 Field
summary:
Defending Champion GM Nodirbek Abdusattorov and GM Javokhir Sindarov, potentially the new world champion after the 2026 FIDE World Championship, top the field for Tata Steel Chess 2027. The fields have been announced for the Masters and Challengers, which run from January 15 to January 31, 2027. The Masters section also includes past winners GMs Levon Aronian (four times!), Jorden van Foreest (2021), and Anish Giri (2023).

Masters Section

The 2027 Masters field. Image: Tata Steel Chess.

The past champions are joined by 2750+ rated GMs Vincent Keymer and Alireza Firouzja. The field also includes two teenage prodigies, GM Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus, a 15-year-old already ranked 21st in the world. Slightly older than Erdogmus, 16-year-old GM Andy Woodward graduates to join the masters after winning the Challengers section last year.

GM Hans Niemann returns to the field after a difficult U.S. Championship appearance. He will have an opportunity to level the score against GM Frederik Svane, who defeated him in a memorable game in the recent Chess Olympiad. GM Nihal Sarin would also like to put a difficult Olympiad behind him. GM Amin Tabatabaei has been moving up the ranks this year, and currently sits at 18th in the world.

Finally, there's one unnamed player in the Masters section. You can expect a strong GM to take that final spot.

Challengers Section

The Challengers section is always a strong tournament, with the top finisher joining next year's Masters tournament.

The 2027 Challengers field. Image: Tata Steel Chess.

The Challengers section has a strong young field.

This list of stars includes Olympiad gold medalists (Madaminov, Lee, and Samunenkov), Women's Candidates participants (Zhu and Assaubayeva), a former 2750-rated player (Aravindh), and a host of young prodigies.

The 89th edition of Tata Steel Chess takes place January 15-31, 2027, in Wijk aan Zee, the Netherlands. Both the Masters and Challengers groups are 14-player round-robin tournaments. The time control is 120 minutes for 40 moves followed by 30 minutes to the end of the game, with a 30-second increment only from move 41. No draw offers were allowed before move 40.

title: Hikaru Nakamura Renews With Chess.com
summary:
GM Hikaru Nakamura, one of the game's leading players and most influential content creators, has renewed with Chess.com, extending a longstanding partnership.

From record-breaking blitz performances to introducing chess to new audiences through streaming and PogChamps, the 38-year-old world number-two has made both competing and creating content part of one incredible chess career.

Hikaru has now signed a new long-term agreement with Chess.com, extending a partnership that began in 2013.

The new chapter in his Chess.com career gets a jump-start with the upcoming Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026, where Hikaru will join the Chess.com commentary team for some key games and comment on the rest of the games on his Kick channel. Fans can also look forward to an exciting Hikaru vs. The World match, set to take place in 2027.

Hikaru Nakamura playing Titled Tuesday during Chess.com's Meetup in Greece. Photo: Chess.com.

"It's been an incredible journey seeing Chess.com grow from a small company with no more than 50 employees to what it is today, and to see the dramatic rise of chess during my time with the company," Hikaru said.

"There have been so many memories and inflection points along the way: Danny, a small-time executive at the time, reaching out to try to convince me to stream; covering the 2018 World Championship with the monkey-clapping memes; the whole golden age of the chess boom in 2020 and 2021, with xQc, Reckful, and other streamers playing chess, culminating in PogChamps and blockbuster TV shows like The Queen's Gambit."

"The whole ride has been amazing to be a part of," he added.

The whole ride has been amazing to be a part of.

—Hikaru Nakamura

Chess.com Chief Chess Officer IM Danny Rensch also welcomed the renewed agreement.

"Hikaru has been with Chess.com through so many wild rides, from every edition of the Speed Chess Championship to the PRO Chess League, and PogChamps, to countless Titled Tuesdays and Bullet Brawls, and so, so much more," he said.

"As a player and creator, he has inspired generations and blazed a trail for those who will come after him. We are so excited to have been partnered with Hikaru for over a decade, and we are thrilled for this next chapter."

Hikaru Nakamura against Magnus Carlsen in Norway Chess 2024. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

With 8.6 million followers across his social media platforms, Hikaru has played a key role in bringing chess to new audiences and helping grow the game's popularity. As a coach and commentator in the first PogChamps, one of the most-watched chess events of all time, he helped make chess approachable for creators and viewers discovering the game together.

His streams, YouTube videos, and shorts have entertained millions, and shown how one of the world's top grandmasters could entertain, teach, and build a community. In doing so, he helped pave the way for the chess creator scene that followed.

One of PogChamps’ most memorable moments came during Hikaru and WFM Alexandra Botez’s commentary of the xQc vs. Moistcr1tikal match, which ended much sooner than either expected. The clip has been viewed more than 26 million times.

And it continued with PogChamps 2.

His streaming career has produced plenty of milestones, and some unusual personal bests:

Most viewers: 84,403 (Magnus Carlsen Invitational, March 16, 2021)

Most new subscribers on a single day: 13,609 (January 8, 2021)

Most bullet games won in an hour: 52 (June 1, 2021)

Best Human Benchmark Chimp Test: 30

Highest Bullet Brawl Score: 320 arena points

Longest Bullet Brawl Streak: 59

Most bananas eaten on stream: 5 (January 2021)

While growing his online streaming and creator career, Hikaru continued to prove himself at the highest level over the board. His achievements include five U.S. Championship titles, victory in the 2011 Tata Steel Chess Masters, 2022 Fischer Random World Championship, the 2023 Norway Chess title, and his bayou-based detour in the 2025 Louisiana State Championship, which paved his road to the Candidates the following year.

This year, Hikaru made his fourth appearance at the FIDE Candidates Tournament, once again competing for a shot at the world championship, while bringing fans along through his YouTube recaps. The videos offered a firsthand account of his games and thought process, combining top-level events with the content creation that has become central to his career.

On Chess.com, his remarkable record spans the platform's biggest championships and its weekly tournaments. He won five consecutive Speed Chess Championships from 2018 through 2022, and has four Bullet Chess Championship titles, including a 17-15 victory over GM Magnus Carlsen in a thrilling 2023 final.

More recently, he pushed the Chess.com blitz rating record to 3503. He also leads Titled Tuesday with an astonishing 94 victories in the 11-round era, and Bullet Brawl's all-time winners list with 73 titles—more than twice the next-highest total.

Whether viewers first encountered him coaching a streamer, winning a Speed Chess final, or explaining a Candidates game, Hikaru has offered them a way into the sport.

With World Championship commentary and Hikaru vs. The World ahead, the renewed partnership will give fans more opportunities to learn from him—and a chance to play against him.

Alongside his appearances on Chess.com's commentary team, Hikaru will cover every day of the Salesforce FIDE World Championship on his Kick channel. Will you be watching?

title: Gukesh-Sindarov Predictions: Kasparov, Nakamura, Carlsen & More
summary:
It's now just two weeks until the Salesforce FIDE World Championship 2026 sees GM Javokhir Sindarov take on World Champion Gukesh Dommaraju for the most important title in chess. On the eve of that showdown in Geneva, we look at some of the predictions from the chess world, including 13th World Champion Garry Kasparov favoring Gukesh slightly, while GM Hikaru Nakamura predicts Sindarov winning "very cleanly."

On paper, the reigning world champion, Gukesh, faces a daunting task in the upcoming match. He's currently 26th in the world, the lowest ranking of a player in a world championship match ever, and 22 spots and 72 rating points behind the challenger, Sindarov.

Rating/Ranking Gap Before World Championship Matches

Year | Player | Rating | Rank | Player | Rating | Rank | Rating Gap | Ranking Gap

2026 | Javokhir Sindarov | 2782 | #4 | Gukesh Dommaraju | 2710 | #26 | 72 | 22

2024 | 🏆 Gukesh Dommaraju | 2783 | #5 | Ding Liren | 2728 | #23 | 55 | 18

2023 | Ian Nepomniachtchi | 2795 | #2 | 🏆 Ding Liren | 2788 | #3 | 7 | 1

2021 | 🏆 Magnus Carlsen | 2856 | #1 | Ian Nepomniachtchi | 2782 | #5 | 74 | 4

2018 | 🏆 Magnus Carlsen | 2835 | #1 | Fabiano Caruana | 2832 | #2 | 3 | 1

2016 | 🏆 Magnus Carlsen | 2853 | #1 | Sergey Karjakin | 2772 | #9 | 81 | 8

2014 | 🏆 Magnus Carlsen | 2863 | #1 | Viswanathan Anand | 2792 | #6 | 71 | 5

2013 | 🏆 Magnus Carlsen | 2870 | #1 | Viswanathan Anand | 2775 | #8 | 95 | 7

2012 | 🏆 Viswanathan Anand | 2791 | #4 | Boris Gelfand | 2727 | #20 | 64 | 16

2010 | Veselin Topalov | 2805 | #2 | 🏆 Viswanathan Anand | 2787 | #4 | 18 | 2

2008 | 🏆 Viswanathan Anand | 2783 | #5 | Vladimir Kramnik | 2772 | #6 | 11 | 1

The lowest a player has been ranked and still won the title since it was unified in 2008 is fifth in the world.

Nevertheless, title matches are unlike anything else in chess, and GM Ding Liren was one late blunder away from forcing tiebreaks against 55-point and 18-place-higher-ranked Gukesh in 2024. Gukesh himself had the best 2024 of any player in the world and as recently as 18 months ago was world number-three, so it would be foolish to doubt the 20-year-old's potential.

Ding Liren came within a whisker of forcing rapid tiebreaks. Photo: Maria Emelianova/Chess.com.

Let's look at some of the predictions heading into the match.

Garry Kasparov

Kasparov was recently in Antwerp, Belgium to give a simultaneous exhibition as part of Your Next Move 2026, during which he gave a press conference, as reported by Sportinantwerpen. Kasparov referred to earlier comments about Gukesh's struggles since winning the title, saying, "Like Magnus Carlsen, I was fiercely critical of him, and that criticism still stands."

He added, however:

As far as I can judge, Sindarov provides more entertainment, but experience is important. And Dommaraju has that. You can hardly beat him. That is why I give him a slightly better chance. It is not important how long you prepare for a match; experience is usually the deciding factor.

Last year in St. Louis, Garry Kasparov once more defeated one of his world championship opponents, Vishy Anand. Photo: Lennart Ootes/Saint Louis Chess Club.

It is not important how long you prepare for a match; experience is usually the deciding factor.

—Garry Kasparov

Kasparov reflected on Gukesh's seven wins and one loss at the FIDE Chess Olympiad in Samarkand:

He didn't make a good impression at the Olympiad, but now it's about a match against a single player. That's completely different. Expectations are high. He is a more defensive player—compare it to a tennis player who doesn't come off the baseline. But you never know, if Sindarov takes the lead, he might just be able to beat him.

A counter-argument was provided by the world number-two.

Hikaru Nakamura

During commentary on round five of the recent U.S. Championships, Nakamura was asked who would win the world championship. He gave a 45-second response, beginning:

I think that if I look at it objectively, I struggle to see Sindarov not winning. I want a close match, but I think most likely the result we're going to get is a match where Sindarov wins very cleanly, like Magnus did against Anand in 2013.

I think most likely the result we're going to get is a match where Sindarov wins very cleanly, like Magnus did against Anand in 2013.

—Hikaru Nakamura

He did add, however:

I think if it’s a close match, Gukesh will actually win, but I don’t think it’s going to be a close match. There’s nothing in Gukesh’s games in the last year and a half that makes me believe that he’s going to suddenly play at a much higher level.

Nakamura and Sindarov spent some time in the same hotel in Cyprus recently.

@GMHikaru @Cap_StGeorges Works quite well https://t.co/y54XQ9x8Rb

— Javokhir Sindarov (@GMJSindarov) October 15, 2026

When they were previously in Cyprus it was for the Candidates Tournament, and many of the opinions the International Chess Federation (FIDE) recently gathered together came shortly after that event.

Notably, Nakamura himself had more hope for Gukesh at the time:

I think if Gukesh can find the form he found in the match and the tournaments leading up to it, he’ll win, and I think as long as he works on the mental aspects and he’s able to drown out the noise, I think he’s going to surprise people.

Among the other views expressed, French GMs Maxime Vachier-Lagrave and Alireza Firouzja both stated 50:50 as their prediction, while IM Levy Rozman gave 55:45 to Sindarov. Sindarov was the clear favorite, given the edge, however slight, by GMs Anish Giri, Divya Deshmukh, Faustino Oro, Juan Manuel Bellon Lopez, as well as WFM Anna Cramling.

Anna's mother GM Pia Cramling opted for Gukesh, but explained "because I've played him," while GM Viswanathan Anand, who did some work for Gukesh before the previous match, mentioned "I'll root for Gukesh." Andrea Botez also chose the Indian reigning champion.

Caruana and Sindarov faced off recently in St. Louis. Photo: Lennart Ootes/Saint Louis Chess Club.

GM Fabiano Caruana, who tied GM Magnus Carlsen in classical chess in the 2018 World Championship match, didn't go against the prevailing opinion, but did explain he expects things to be close:

I should say Javokhir. Of course after this [Candidates] result and his form is so good, but I don’t think it’ll be easy. I know that people are putting very high odds on him because he’s super-hot at the moment. Gukesh is having a rough period, but I still think it’ll be very close.

We got a similar view from another strong and experienced player.

Peter Svidler

GM Peter Svidler was asked after Gukesh scored 8.5/11 at the Olympiad, with only a last-round loss denying him a third individual gold medal in a row. The eight-time Russian champion commented, "Winning games of chess is what makes you feel better about yourself, and he won a great number here."

When Svidler was asked about how the players' styles compared, he pointed out, "people who reach this level are pretty much always universals," before noting that chess has changed with the computer. He explained:

Their formative years were spent working with computers and that, I think, very much changes how they view the game, because if there's one thing that computers teach you forcefully, time and time again, it is that a lot more is affordable, a lot more is defensible, a lot more is possible if you can just calculate really, really cleanly. It’s a lot more natural to them to play dynamic chess than it is to play positional chess. They’re still universals, but I think they're slightly less universal than the previous generations because of the amount of work they do with computers from a very early age.

Svidler, a Hearthstone fanatic, is heartened by Sindarov's love of Counter-Strike:

I know a little bit about the approach of this current crop of Indian youngsters to video games. There is not going to be any Counter-Strike on that side of the equation, I can pretty much guarantee that. As for Javokhir, it was very gratifying and a happy moment for me when I realized he is a fellow gamer, and I do hope he maintains some sort of work-life balance and then does well, because that would sort of retrospectively slightly justify my life choices.

I do hope he maintains some sort of work-life balance and then does well, because that would sort of retrospectively slightly justify my life choices.

—Peter Svidler on Javokhir Sindarov

As for the players' chances and whether it was 60:40 for Sindarov, Svidler responded:

For these matches, 60 is already very high. Even with the kind of a year and a half Gukesh has had I don’t think going higher than 55 is justifiable. He's still a very strong player, it's still a very specific format, so I'm kind of willing to go 55:45 Sindarov, but I don't think I'm willing to go higher.

That brings us to an Indian player who Svidler has seconded in the Candidates.

Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu

GM Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Gukesh obviously get on very well, which has provoked questions about whether they're collaborating for the match.

The most expected collab in chess - best buddies Gukesh and Praggnanandhaa! Video: Pragg and Gukesh's instagram https://t.co/m14b3Aztwb

— ChessBase India (@ChessbaseIndia) September 28, 2026

We'll probably only get confirmation when it's over, but Praggnanandhaa is another player to put the odds for who'll win at 50:50. In an interview with Chess.com he gave two factors that work in Gukesh's favor. The first was how quickly things can change in chess.

I honestly think it's 50:50. I don't think there's any one massive favorite. Obviously Gukesh's form hasn't been the best, but it's always one tournament, or even one game, to get that confidence and form back. Even for me—if you had seen me till Norway round six, I think everyone would be saying Pragg is not in great shape, and then four days later I won the tournament. So it's always a few games, or just one game, to get that confidence, and then we all know what Gukesh is capable of—he's really shown it at the top level.

We all know what Gukesh is capable of—he's really shown it at the top level.

—Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu

The other is the pressure of playing your first title match.

And for Javokhir as well—the first few games in a World Championship match, everyone knows how much pressure it is, but no one has actually experienced it, so it will be a new experience for him, and that's also going to play a role.

One player who does know all there is to know about playing such matches is the world number-one.

Magnus Carlsen

After Sindarov won the Candidates, Carlsen was asked who would win the match and, on a big screen in Sweden, replied "at the moment it's impossible not to say Sindarov."

🇺🇿 Sindarov or 🇮🇳 Gukesh? 🇳🇴 Magnus shared his thoughts at the Chess Party in Stockholm. https://t.co/HvQYaxsFMN

— International Chess Federation (@FIDE_chess) April 19, 2026

He elaborated: "Gukesh has very, very obvious weaknesses when it comes to his understanding, and Sindarov does not in the same way. He’s a lot more well-rounded."

Gukesh has very, very obvious weaknesses when it comes to understanding, and Sindarov does not in the same way.

—Magnus Carlsen

During the Tech Mahindra Global Chess League, Carlsen returned to the topic. The Norwegian said of Gukesh, "He’s a very good player, he had a fantastic 2024, one of the best years that anybody’s ever had," but feels Sindarov is a "pretty significant favorite."

He noted Gukesh "doesn't find it easy to just switch gears," and has often been punished for his ambition:

I don’t think it’s a secret to most people that his evaluations are way too optimistic. That kind of makes him take way more chances than he should. I think especially now that his confidence hasn't been too high, he just tries to do a little bit too much.

Will Gukesh tone down his style for the match, or will he manage to make it work when it matters most? Who do you think will win?

The Sal

title: Unbeaten Carlsen wins opening blitz as Total Chess Pilot gets underway in Budapest
summary: The world’s best opened the pilot with nine rounds of 3+2 blitz, the first of the three disciplines that will decide the most complete player in Budapest. World No. 1 Magnus Carlsen won the nine-round Blitz Swiss that opened the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot on Tuesday evening, finishing unbeaten on 7/9 at the Anantara New York Palace Budapest Hotel. Maxime Vachier-Lagrave took second place on 6.5 points, and Levon Aronian finished third on 6. Carlsen settled it in the final round, beating Haik Martirosyan with the black pieces while Vachier-Lagrave was held to a draw by Hans Niemann. Kjell Madland, CEO of Total Chess, and FIDE President Timur Turlov opened the day with welcoming speeches and then set the competition in motion by making the first ceremonial moves in the game Magnus Carlsen – Jan-Krzysztof Duda. Carlsen and Vachier-Lagrave set the pace all evening. Carlsen reached the final round unbeaten on 6/8. He defeated Jan-Krzysztof Duda, Richard Rapport, Arjun Erigaisi and Anish Giri, and drew with Vachier-Lagrave, Ian Nepomniachtchi, Niemann and Levon Aronian. Vachier-Lagrave drew level with him by beating Alireza Firouzja in round 8, but could not match Carlsen’s last-round win. The opening night’s ranking will follow the players all the way to the final day. It breaks ties in the group stage, decides the semifinal pairings in all six knockout brackets, and gives the higher-ranked player the choice of colour in the first blitz game of every knockout match. Carlsen has taken the first advantage of the tournament. Erigaisi was the only player to defeat Vachier-Lagrave, and his win over Fabiano Caruana in round 8 took him into the final round half a point off the lead. In the last round, Aronian beat him to take third place, completing a run of four wins from his last six games. Erigaisi finished in a five-way tie for fourth on 5.5 points with Firouzja, Caruana, Niemann and Rapport. The first upset of the night came in round 1, when home favourite Rapport, Hungary’s highest-rated player, beat world No. 3 Caruana. He closed the evening with a win over Vladislav Artemiev to finish on 5.5. Vaishali R produced two of the night’s standout results, beating Niemann in the opening round and Wesley So in round 3. Praggnanandhaa R, the reigning Norway Chess champion, closed with a win over Andrew Hong to finish on 4.5 points, with Vaishali on 4. The drawing of lots earlier in the day settled the groups for the Fast Classic stage. Group B looks the deepest on paper, with three of the world’s top ten in Caruana, Praggnanandhaa and Vincent Keymer, along with Rapport. Carlsen faces Giri, Nepomniachtchi and Shakhriyar Mamedyarov in Group C, while Group D brings together So, Erigaisi, Vachier-Lagrave, and Niemann with Bibisara Assaubayeva and Vaishali, the two women in the field. Group A: Alireza Firouzja, Jorden van Foreest, Andrew Hong, Jan-Krzysztof Duda, Levon Aronian, Nodirbek Abdusattorov Group B: Vladislav Artemiev, Richard Rapport, Praggnanandhaa R, Vincent Keymer, Fabiano Caruana, Liem Le Group C: Anish Giri, Haik M. Martirosyan, Ian Nepomniachtchi, Abhimanyu Mishra, Shakhriyar Mamedyarov, Magnus Carlsen Group D: Vaishali R, Hans Niemann, Bibisara Assaubayeva, Wesley So, Arjun Erigaisi, Maxime Vachier-Lagrave Blitz Swiss, top eight: 1. Magnus Carlsen 7; 2. Maxime Vachier-Lagrave 6.5; 3. Levon Aronian 6; joint 4th on 5.5: Arjun Erigaisi, Alireza Firouzja, Fabiano Caruana, Hans Niemann and Richard Rapport, with tiebreaks deciding their order. Full standings: totalchess.com/tournaments/budapest-2026 The Fast Classic group stage starts on Wednesday, November 11, with two rounds a day at 15:00 and 18:30 CET. Each group plays a double round robin at 45 minutes plus 30 seconds per move, and with three points for a win and one for a draw, playing for the full point is highly incentivized. Only the four group winners reach the title bracket, but nobody goes home: every player moves on to a knockout bracket, and places 5 to 24 are also decided over the board. A total of $650,000 in prize money is at stake. The tournament reaches more than 200 countries and territories. DAZN is the worldwide broadcast partner, and NDTV brings the event to Indian audiences on television and digital platforms, including YouTube. Fans can also follow it on Chess.com, ChessBase India, TV 2 in Norway and the Norway Chess YouTube channel. Anna Rudolf, Fiona Steil-Antoni, David Howell and Jovanka Houska lead the main broadcast, with Levy Rozman hosting the Total Chess Highlight Show. About the format The Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot introduces a groundbreaking competition format designed to identify the world’s most complete chess player by combining Fast Classic, Rapid and Blitz into a single championship. The pilot event brings together 24 elite players, who begin the tournament in a group stage comprising four groups of six players each. Every group follows a double round-robin format over five days, with players contesting ten Fast Classic games (45 minutes plus a 30-second increment). Victories earn three points, while draws are worth one point. A nine-round Blitz Swiss tournament held before the competition determines tie-break rankings. Following the group stage, players progress into knockout brackets based on their finishing positions. Each knockout match is played over two days and tests competitors across all three disciplines, with four Blitz games (3+2), two Rapid games (15+10) and one Fast Classic game (45+30) each day, and weighted scoring rewarding success in longer formats. The four highest-ranked players across the Tour qualify for the Grand Final, where semifinals and the championship match determine the inaugural FIDE World Combined Champion. Should a knockout match remain tied, an Armageddon game is used to decide the winner, ensuring every contest produces a definitive result. The format rewards consistency, versatility and excellence across every major discipline of elite chess. Three disciplines. One champion. One global tour. The journey begins in Budapest. For more information, visit: www.totalchess.com Text: Total Chess Photos: Total Chess / Michal Walusza About Total Chess Total Chess is a global championship platform established to redefine elite competitive chess for the modern era.

title: WACC 2026: Aqil reaches 6/6 as Tulegenov regains sole lead in Klang
summary: Klang, Selangor, Malaysia, 10 November 2026 – Malaysia’s Aqil Ainuddin Naufal Akhramsyah Muammar Ubaidah extended his perfect run to six victories in Open Under-2000, while Kazakhstan’s Amir Tulegenov regained the outright lead in Open Under-2300 following Round 6 of the FIDE World Amateur Chess Championships 2026. Photo: Ozgur Solakoglu, honorary chairman of the FIDE Event Commission, making the ceremonial first move of Round 6 The sixth round, played on the afternoon of November 9, completed a demanding double-round day at the KSL Esplanade Hotel. With three rounds remaining, several title races remain closely contested across the six championship sections. Open U2300: Tulegenov wins the leaders’ clash Amir Tulegenov defeated Vietnam’s CM Tran Pham Quang Minh with the black pieces in the clash between the joint leaders. The victory lifted Tulegenov to 5½/6, restoring his half-point advantage at the top. Malaysia’s FM Genivan Genkeswaran and Colombia’s FM Nestor Favian Lozano Ramirez share second place on 5/6. Genkeswaran defeated Kazakhstan’s Adil Tkachyov, while Lozano Ramirez overcame Uzbekistan’s Avazbek Ishbaev. India’s Gopal Krishna Maheshwari, Vietnam’s CM Tran Pham Quang Minh, Mongolia’s FM Bayarmandakh Balgan and Malaysia’s Leong Khai Shen follow on 4½/6. Women’s U2300: Pavithra moves into first place Pavithra R V of India took the sole lead in the ten-player round-robin after defeating Mongolia’s WFM Saikhanchimeg Tsogtsaikhan with Black. She remains unbeaten on 5/6. Malaysia’s WCM Nithyalakshmi Sivanesan continued her impressive run by defeating India’s WCM Pooja Shree R, having beaten the previous leader, WCM Mumtozbegim Mansurova, in the morning round. Nithyalakshmi joins Bulgaria’s WFM Patricie Naymanova and Uzbekistan’s WCM Mumtozbegim Mansurova on 4½/6. Naymanova defeated Zambia’s WFM Constance Mbatha, while Mansurova returned to winning ways against Mongolia’s WFM Khuslenzaya Baldanjantsan. Pavithra is scheduled to face Nithyalakshmi in Round 7, an important encounter between the leader and one of her closest challengers. Open U2000: Aqil extends his perfect streak Aqil Ainuddin Naufal Akhramsyah Muammar Ubaidah strengthened his title challenge with a sixth consecutive victory, defeating Anatoly Fridman, competing under the FIDE flag, with the black pieces. His perfect 6/6 gives him a full-point lead over three challengers: G Kavinkumar (IND) — 5/6 Mukhammadrizo Umarov (UZB) — 5/6 Munkhbaatar Surenmandakh (MNG) — 5/6 Kavinkumar defeated Malaysia’s Irfan Harith Rosli, Umarov prevailed over India’s C Maniswar, and Munkhbaatar drew with Vietnam’s Hoang Minh Hieu. Women’s U2000: Osadchuk opens a one-point gap Anastasiia Osadchuk (UKR) recorded another important victory, defeating Mongolia’s Naranzaya Zorigoo to reach 5½/6. She remains unbeaten and now leads the section by a full point. Mongolia’s WCM Odmaa Enkhsaikhan moved into clear second place on 4½/6 after defeating her compatriot Munkh-Ayalguu Dorjderem. Naranzaya, Bulgaria’s Stefani Chuchukova, and Malaysia’s Ashwiniy Kumaran and Nur Ain Shahar share third place on 4/6. Open U1700: Suwanto and Javkhlan stay perfect Joel Wilson Suwanto (IDN) and Javkhlan Bayarjargal (MNG) share the lead with perfect scores of 6/6. Suwanto defeated fellow overnight co-leader Gankhuleg Gurragchaa of Mongolia, while Javkhlan overcame Malaysia’s Firast Haiqal Mohd Firdaus. Five players form the chasing group on 5/6: Gankhuleg Gurragchaa (MNG) Munkhbat Batnyam (MNG) Altair Kassymov (KAZ) Arulan Izgugaliyev (KAZ) Tang Keran (CHN) Women’s U1700: Leading pair keeps winning Dolgormaa Lkhavgasuren (MNG) and Tan Sue Anne (MYS) both won to remain joint leaders on 5½/6. Dolgormaa defeated India’s Disha U A, while Tan won over Vietnam’s Truong Tran Loan Ngoc. Both leaders remain unbeaten, having drawn their direct encounter in Round 5. Mongolia’s Sod-Erdene Naranbaatar follows on 5/6 after defeating compatriot WCM Tenuunbuyan Sukhbaatar. Malaysia’s Ashreeya Rao Sangkaran and India’s S Sreenanda are close behind on 4½/6. Three rounds to decide the titles Round 7 is scheduled for Tuesday, 10 November, at 16:00, Malaysian time. Round 8 follows on 11 November, with the ninth and final round scheduled for 12 November at 10:00. The championships are organized by the Selangor Chess Association under the auspices of FIDE and the Malaysian Chess Federation, with Open and Women’s competitions in the Under-2300, Under-2000, and Under-1700 categories.
